title: The Evening Brief: Sector Layoffs Accelerate as Courts and Regulators Test Federal Crypto Authority
dek: Anchorage Digital cut 17% of its workforce Sunday, joining a sector-wide contraction that has shed tens of thousands of jobs in 2026. Meanwhile, a federal court challenge to the OCC's crypto trust charters and an emergency pause on Arbitrum's Stylus contracts signal mounting pressure on the regulatory and technical foundations built over the past year.
author: Crypto Cronkite
key_fact: The crypto sector is contracting sharply on headcount even as institutional adoption accelerates, while the legal and operational infrastructure underpinning custody and smart-contract execution faces simultaneous stress tests from litigation and security incidents.
bottom_line: The desk's Whale Watch board shows $111.6 million in value moving off exchanges over 48 hours, led by $58.0 million in bitcoin from okex and $53.6 million in ethereum from bitfinex; over the same window, the week ending October 4 recorded $804 million moving onto exchanges. ETF flows diverge: bitcoin shows an inflow of $31.7 million on October 2 and a net inflow of $82.9 million over the last five sessions; ethereum shows an outflow of $17.3 million on October 2 and a net outflow of $118.0 million over the last five sessions. The data reflects month-to-date strength tested by near-term pullback and mixed institutional appetite. Coming checkpoints: the ICBA's federal court challenge to the OCC's trust bank rule and the SEC's response timeline, Arbitrum Security Council's decision on when to reopen Stylus activations, Iran's central bank account block enforcement date if it materializes, and whether the October 3-4 expiration of Iran's temporary Tether trading limits extends into permanent restrictions.
body: Anchorage Digital, the first federally chartered US digital asset bank, cut 17% of its workforce this week, roughly 68 jobs out of a global staff of approximately 400 as of February 2025, per McCauley's congressional testimony. As the desk reported, the layoff marks the second major reduction at the company, following a 20% cut in 2023. The move arrives despite regulatory approvals and institutional inflows that the reporting notes suggest stability, underscoring a deeper pattern: the sector is contracting sharply on headcount even as some institutional pathways widen.

Anchorage is not alone. The reporting documents a wave of sector-wide cuts: Gemini trimmed about 30% of its workforce; Crypto.com cut 12% in March; Coinbase announced elimination of about 700 roles, or 14% of staff, in May; Dune laid off 25% in May; Luno trimmed 20% in July; Bitwise cut about 14% in August; and BitMEX, Lisk, and Blast announced complete shutdowns. The broader tech sector is contracting too. US tech firms announced 10,799 cuts in September, up 77% from August; tech has announced 165,925 cuts in 2026 so far, up 54% from a year earlier, and now accounts for 29% of all US job cut announcements.

Simultaneously, the regulatory infrastructure crypto firms depend on is under legal challenge. The Independent Community Bankers of America sued the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency on October 2 in federal court in Washington, seeking to vacate the OCC's national trust bank rule and Interpretive Letter 1176. As the desk reported, the ICBA argues the agency exceeded its authority by widening limited-purpose trust charters for fintech and crypto firms. The OCC has approved or conditionally approved 21 trust banks since December 2025, 13 of them tied to crypto. The suit targets Protego's conditional approval and seeks to prevent further charters. The OCC finalized its rule citing the Supreme Court's Loper Light decision, signaling confidence it expected litigation and believed it had sufficient authority; how the court interprets the National Bank Act's scope will determine whether the national trust bank becomes a firmer federal route for crypto custody and stablecoin infrastructure, or whether those services migrate to state trusts or partnership arrangements.

On the technical side, Arbitrum's Security Council executed an emergency protocol safeguard on October 2 by temporarily blocking new Stylus contract activations on Arbitrum One and Nova, per CryptoSlate reporting. The move restricts new programs and app updates that require fresh activation but leaves already-active Stylus applications running and ordinary Solidity contract deployment unaffected. Arbitrum attributed the precaution to increasingly sophisticated AI-assisted attacks involving hand-crafted WebAssembly programs outside the standard Stylus compiler toolchain. The Council raised the activation gas requirement to a prohibitively expensive level. The reporting does not specify when activations will reopen, but notes the defining consequence for developers is whether the pause extends beyond weeks, as longer periods may force abandonment of projects requiring fresh activation or version updates.

International enforcement continued Sunday. Japan added Garantex, a Moscow-based cryptocurrency exchange, to its official sanctions list effective October 2, 2026, joining the United States and European Union in designating the platform. The action broadens enforcement posture but, as the reporting notes, Garantex is already operationally offline; the significance rests on whether Japan and other jurisdictions will extend sanctions lists to cover alleged successor entities at the pace those entities appear.

Iran's central bank is moving to sever rial bank accounts and payment gateways from domestic crypto exchanges including Nobitex and Wallex, according to Crypto Briefing. The stated rationale is concern over market manipulation. The action escalates curbs introduced in late September, when the central bank capped Tether purchases at 2,000 USDT per user per day and suspended trading nightly on those platforms; those temporary restrictions were set to expire around October 3 to 4. If the planned account blocks proceed, they would strike deeper, cutting off the banking rails that allow exchanges to convert rials into crypto. The reporting does not confirm an enforcement date, final scope of affected exchanges, or mechanism of implementation. The central bank's simultaneous custody of $507 million in USDT while restricting retail access creates a credibility risk if Tether freezes more holdings.
